title: Concession & reasons — 〜のに vs 〜ので, 〜ても/〜でも, 〜し

grammarPoints.rule: のに and ので (module 16, id node-because) are built from the exact same joint — hang on the plain form, な after a noun or な-adjective, never だ — which is exactly why they're easy to mix up. ので presents a reason as simply how things are: neutral, matter-of-fact. のに presents the OPPOSITE relationship: not a reason, a CONTRADICTION, and it never leaves the room emotionally neutral. 「たかいのに かった」 isn't just 'it was expensive, and I bought it' — it carries a little shrug, almost a confession: it was expensive, and yet I bought it anyway. Whatever follows のに has to CLASH with what came before it; ので never asks that of its second half.

examples.ja: たかいのに かった。
examples.en: It was expensive, and yet I bought it.

examples.ja: がんばったのに おちた。
examples.en: I tried hard, and yet I failed.

examples.ja: むりなのに、やった。
examples.en: It was unreasonable, and yet I did it.

examples.ja: じかんが ないのに、いった。
examples.en: I had no time, and yet I went.

antiPattern.ja: たかいので かった。
antiPattern.why: ので reports this as a flat, reasoned fact — nothing clashes, no shrug. のに is what carries the contradiction: it was expensive, and yet I bought it anyway: たかいのに かった。

grammarPoints.rule: Now push のに into the register it actually lives in: complaint. Every real use of のに carries some flavor of disapproval, surprise, or reproach — you had every reason NOT to do the thing, and did it anyway, and the sentence says so. 「ねつが あるのに がっこうに いった」 isn't neutral reporting; it's the sentence a worried friend says next: you had a fever, and you WENT? That emotional colour is not optional decoration on のに — it is what のに means. A gloss that reads perfectly flat ('I had a fever and went to school') is a sign you've drifted toward ので's job, not のに's.

examples.ja: ねつが あるのに がっこうに いった。
examples.en: I had a fever, and yet I went to school.

examples.ja: ひまなのに、いえに いる。
examples.en: Even though I'm free, I'm staying home.

examples.ja: きたないのに、すきだ。
examples.en: It's dirty, and yet I like it.

examples.ja: うるさいのに、がんばった。
examples.en: It was noisy, and yet I did my best.

antiPattern.ja: ねつが あるので がっこうに いった。
antiPattern.why: ので reports this as a flat, reasoned choice — no fever, no clash, nothing a worried friend would remark on. のに is what carries the 'and yet you WENT?' feeling: ねつが あるのに がっこうに いった。

grammarPoints.rule: 〜ても is concession over an action or a quality — 'even if / even though'. The form is already yours: て(module 8) glued to a verb or an い-adjective, plus も(module 3). たかい → たかくて → たかくても. The only new piece is the MEANING. のに reports something that already happened and already clashed — a done contradiction, always a little sour. ても reaches forward into something not yet decided, or something generally true, and holds regardless: 「たかくても かう」 = even if it's expensive, I'll buy it — resolve, not regret. 「あめが ふっても いく」 = even if it rains, I'll go. The clause after ても doesn't have to be sour at all; it can be plain determination.

examples.ja: たかくても かう。
examples.en: Even if it's expensive, I'll buy it.

examples.ja: あめが ふっても いく。
examples.en: Even if it rains, I'll go.

examples.ja: いそがしくても てつだう。
examples.en: Even though I'm busy, I'll help.

antiPattern.why: ても needs the て-form underneath it — たかい bends to たかくて first. Bare たかい plus も skips that step and isn't a word: たかくても かう。

grammarPoints.rule: でも does for nouns and な-adjectives what ても does for verbs and い-adjectives: concession, 'even'. Attach で (the copula's connecting shape) plus も directly to the noun or な-adjective: 「がくせいでも わかる」 = even a student understands; 「ひまでも いかない」 = even though I'm free, I won't go. One warning, mechanical not semantic: this でも is NOT the sentence-starting でも you already know ('but', its own sentence). Same two kana, different job — that one opens a brand-new sentence; this one glues onto a word inside one clause.

examples.ja: がくせいでも わかる。
examples.en: Even a student understands.

examples.ja: ひまでも いかない。
examples.en: Even though I'm free, I won't go.

examples.ja: あめでも いく。
examples.en: Even if it's rain, I'll go.

antiPattern.ja: がくせいても わかる。
antiPattern.why: ても attaches to a て-form; がくせい is a noun with no て-form to attach to at all. Nouns and な-adjectives take でも instead: がくせいでも わかる。

grammarPoints.rule: A closed set, memorized whole, not derived live: question-word + でも or + も. なんでも = anything, だれでも = anyone, どこでも = anywhere — the でも family means 'no matter which, it doesn't matter.' Flip でも to も with a NEGATIVE verb and the same question words swing to the opposite extreme: だれも いない = nobody is there (not 'anybody is there'), なにも たべない = I'm not eating anything. Ship exactly these five — なんでも/だれでも/どこでも/だれも/なにも — and no others; the course does not derive でも-mo compounds from a productive rule.

examples.en: I'll eat anything.

examples.en: I'm not eating anything.

antiPattern.why: なに shifts to なん before でも/も in this fixed set — なんでも, not なにでも. The other four (だれでも/どこでも/だれも/なにも) keep their bare stem; なに is the one that changes shape.

grammarPoints.rule: The test for telling のに and ので apart: swap in an English connector and see which one keeps the sentence's LOGIC intact. If 'because' fits, it's ので — a plain consequence, no tension. 「あめなので いえに いる」 = it's raining, so I'm staying home; nothing clashes. If 'even though' fits, it's のに — a contradiction. 「あめなのに こうえんに いった」 = it was raining, and yet I went to the park; rain and going-to-the-park don't belong together, and that clash is the whole point. Watch the SECOND half: a plain consequence of the first half is ので's job; anything that fights the first half is のに's.

examples.ja: あめなので いえに いる。
examples.en: It's raining, so I'm staying home.

examples.ja: あめなのに こうえんに いった。
examples.en: It was raining, and yet I went to the park.

examples.ja: じかんが ないのに いった。
examples.en: I had no time, and yet I went.

examples.ja: じかんが ないので いかなかった。
examples.en: I had no time, so I didn't go.

antiPattern.ja: あめなのに いえに いる。
antiPattern.why: Raining and staying home aren't in conflict — that's exactly what you'd expect, a plain consequence, ので's job. のに would claim a contradiction that isn't there: あめなので いえに いる is the sentence this actually is.

grammarPoints.rule: 〜し lists reasons the way English 'and, what's more' does: plain form plus し, piling reasons toward one conclusion, with the flavor that there's more where that came from. 「おいしいし、やすいし、ほしい」 = it's tasty, and what's more it's cheap, so I want it — two reasons stacked, then the payoff. Same joint as から/ので/けど — plain form, な after a noun or な-adjective — but a different job: not ONE reason (から/ので) and not a contrast (けど), a PILE of reasons all pointing the same direction.

examples.ja: おいしいし、やすいし、ほしい。
examples.en: It's tasty, and what's more it's cheap, so I want it.

examples.ja: しずかだし、べんりだし、すきだ。
examples.en: It's quiet, and what's more it's convenient, so I like it.

examples.ja: あめだし、さむいし、いえに いる。
examples.en: It's raining, and what's more it's cold, so I'm staying home.

antiPattern.ja: おいしいから、やすいから、ほしい。
antiPattern.why: から states one reason and stops — repeating it doesn't chain the way し does. Stacking reasons with the 'and what's more' feel needs し: おいしいし、やすいし、ほしい。

beats.en: Even though I'm tired, I'll go.
beats.explanation: ても holds the plan steady regardless of being tired — a concession about something not yet decided. のに would need the going to have already happened and clash with the tiredness. し would just add tiredness as ANOTHER reason pointing the same way — the opposite relationship, not a concession at all.

turns.explanation: し stacks the two reasons with 'and what's more'. やすいから/べんりだから would each give only ONE reason and stop — the pile-up feeling is exactly what し adds that から can't.
